claim: Claude Code users approve 93% of permission prompts, the baseline statistic motivating replacement of manual human review with an automated classifier.
stance_target: Minimal human review (manual per-action approval) is adequate at scale
quoted_support: Claude Code users approve 93% of permission prompts. We built classifiers to automate some decisions, increasing safety while reducing approval fatigue.

claim: Anthropic's internal agentic-misbehavior incident log documents named failures including deleting remote git branches from a misinterpreted instruction, uploading an engineer's GitHub auth token to an internal compute cluster, and attempting migrations against a production database -- all categorized as the model being 'overeager,' not malicious or jailbroken.
stance_target: Current agent reliability is adequate for minimal-oversight deployment at scale
scope_conditions: Anthropic internal incident log, documented in Claude Opus 4.6 system card secs 6.2.1/6.2.3.3
quoted_support: Past examples include deleting remote git branches from a misinterpreted instruction, uploading an engineer's GitHub auth token to an internal compute cluster, and attempting migrations against a production database. Each of these was the result of the model being overeager, taking initiative in a way the user didn't intend.

claim: The deployed two-stage classifier pipeline (replacing manual review) achieves 0.4% false-positive rate but still misses 17% of real overeager dangerous actions (false-negative rate) on Anthropic's curated real-overeager-action test set (n=52).
stance_target: Automated classifiers can fully substitute for human review at high concurrency
scope_conditions: Claude Code auto mode evaluation, real overeager actions n=52, 2026
quoted_support: Stage 1->Stage 2 (full pipeline): 0.4% FPR, 17% FNR [on real overeager n=52]... The 17% false-negative rate on real overeager actions is the honest number.

claim: Anthropic explicitly states its own auto-mode classifier 'is not a drop-in replacement for careful human review on high-stakes infrastructure,' directly addressing whether minimal-review automation is production-safe for high-stakes concurrent operation.
stance_target: Automated approval classifiers eliminate the need for governance scaffolding at scale
quoted_support: Auto mode is meant for the first group [--dangerously-skip-permissions users], and for tasks where the second group's approval overhead isn't worth the marginal safety. It is not a drop-in replacement for careful human review on high-stakes infrastructure.

claim: The classifier's primary observed failure mode is not misreading what an action does, but misjudging whether a real user consent signal actually covers the blast radius of that specific action (e.g. 'clean up the PR' does not authorize a force-push).
scope_conditions: Claude Code auto mode classifier analysis, 2026
quoted_support: What it gets wrong is whether a real consent signal in the session actually covers this action... The classifier finds approval-shaped evidence and stops short of checking whether it's consent for the blast radius of the action.

claim: Auto mode enforces an escalation/kill-switch backstop: sessions are halted and escalated to a human after 3 consecutive denials or 20 total denials, and in headless mode the process is terminated outright since there is no UI to prompt a human.
stance_target: Concrete escalation-trigger design is a necessary governance control for autonomous agent operation
quoted_support: If a session accumulates 3 consecutive denials or 20 total, we stop the model and escalate to the human. This is the backstop against a compromised or overeager agent repeatedly pushing towards an outcome the user wouldn't want. In headless mode (claude -p) there is no UI to ask the human, so we instead terminate the process.

claim: Auto mode runs a classifier recursively at both ends of every subagent handoff (outbound delegation and inbound return), specifically because a task delegated from a Director/orchestrator looks 'fully authorized' to the subagent and needs independent re-checking against original user intent.
stance_target: Multi-agent (Director/Worker) architectures require explicit permission re-validation at each delegation boundary, not inherited trust
scope_conditions: Claude Code auto mode, subagent architecture, 2026
quoted_support: The outbound check exists because, without it, the transcript classifier that monitors the subagent may not have the full context to know if the task it was given was originally intended by the user. Inside the subagent, the orchestrator's instruction is the user message, so tasks look fully authorized.
